claims.text: The initial alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr state is a metastable single-phase beta-BCC solid solution.
The random HfNbTaTiZr alloy has severe lattice distortion caused by atomic-size mismatch and random chemical distribution.
Monte Carlo-based equilibration can generate varying degrees of chemical short-range order.
SRO in HfNbTaTiZr preferentially forms HfTi and TiZr binary clusters.
The HfTi and TiZr clusters undergo a percolative transition into ordered B2-like structures.
An intermediate-temperature regime can support strong SRO while remaining above the long-range-ordering transition.
The percolative transition requires a single-phase BCC matrix.
B2-like binary clusters embedded in the BCC matrix reduce local lattice distortion and atomic displacement amplitudes relative to the random alloy.
Reduced local lattice distortion decreases the scattering of high-frequency phonons.
Ordered B2-like phases have lower high-frequency phonon scattering cross-sections than the severely distorted random alloy.
Percolating ordered clusters create continuous pathways with lower phonon scattering rates.
Ordering sharpens and reduces the broadening of high-frequency phonon DOS features relative to the random alloy.
The modified high-frequency phonon DOS favors longer phonon mean free paths.
Percolative SRO and B2-like ordering increase lattice thermal conductivity relative to the random solid-solution state.
The random HfNbTaTiZr solid solution has low thermal conductivity because random arrangements and severe lattice distortion strongly scatter phonons.
A conductivity increase occurs only after the ordered SRO clusters form a material-spanning percolative network.
Isolated, nonpercolating SRO clusters decrease conductivity because their boundaries introduce additional phonon scattering.
A decrease in atomic displacement amplitudes and sharpening of high-frequency DOS without an increase in thermal conductivity would falsify the proposed causal mechanism.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that nonpercolating clusters should decrease conductivity, whereas the falsification experiment says that observing nonpercolation together with decreased conductivity would falsify the hypothesis. That observation would instead agree with the stated boundary condition.
